query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-principal-element nanoalloys heated to 600–1200 °C under an inert atmosphere, high configurational entropy coupled with local chemical fluctuations stabilizes a single- or dual-phase structure by reducing the driving force for phase segregation, thereby preserving both chemical homogeneity and grain size at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloy powders (equiatomic or near-equiatomic) with a uniform, fine-grained microstructure and minimal oxide content.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary element ratios (e.g., altering Al content from 0.1 to 0.3 in a quinary high-entropy nanoalloy) while subjecting samples to prolonged annealing under inert gas to elevate temperatures from 600 to 1200 °C.
generation.conditions: In-situ high-temperature electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction are used to monitor phase evolution and structural changes; atomistic simulations using representative embedded atom method potentials are employed in parallel to probe atomic-scale interactions under the same thermal conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range order impacted by compositional heterogeneity and entropic stabilization of solid solutions or stable two-phase mixtures (e.g., B2 + disordered BCC).
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy lowers the free energy difference between competing phases, while the varied atomic sizes decrease diffusion and promote local lattice distortions. These factors collectively suppress large-scale phase separation and grain growth when exposed to elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline low-entropy alloy of similar average composition, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit slower grain growth (by a factor of ~2 or more) and maintain a coherent or partially coherent phase assemblage across the 600–1200 °C range, whereas the baseline counterpart will develop extensive phase separation and coarsening under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: An alloy with fewer principal elements (e.g., ternary) of comparable composition but lower configurational entropy, exposed to an identical thermal profile in the same inert atmosphere.
generation.boundary: The prediction holds for multi-principal-element nanoalloys with near-equiatomic mixtures and minimal volatile species under inert conditions and uniform fine-grained starting microstructures. Demonstrable phase changes may accelerate outside the 600–1200 °C range or under non-inert environments.
generation.uncertainty: Exact timescales for onset of microstructural changes are not fully constrained, and compositional extremes refer to approximate atomic ratios, given potential variations in local chemical ordering.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoalloy specimens: one set with near-equiatomic high-entropy compositions and one with reduced elemental diversity. Expose both sets to isothermal soaks at 600, 900, and 1200 °C for extended times. Characterize the microstructure evolution in real time with in-situ high-temperature electron microscopy and ex-situ X-ray diffraction.
measurements: Grain size distribution from electron microscopy
Local chemical composition measurements (EDS or atom probe)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the high-entropy nanoalloy specimen undergoes comparable or faster grain growth, phase decomposition, or chemical segregation relative to the lower-entropy baseline under the same conditions.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] . chosen.why: A combined experimental and computational study directly addresses the open question of what governs structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperatures. By systematically varying alloy composition and thermal loading, real-time observations via advanced microscopy and diffraction can reveal phase evolution and interfacial changes, while simulations provide mechanistic insight into atomistic driving forces and allow exploration of parameter space. This synergy most directly fills the niche regarding the mechanism of high-entropy nanoalloy stability.
